chunks: "A debugger is a tool that lets me control and observe a program while it runs on the target.
With it I can halt the processor, step through code line by line, set breakpoints, look at and change variables, registers and memory, and see the call stack.
It's really a chain of three pieces. On my PC there's the debugger software, in an IDE or GDB, which understands my source code and symbols.
It talks over USB to a debug probe, like an ST-Link or J-Link. The probe talks to the microcontroller over a two-wire SWD interface, or four-wire JTAG.
And inside the chip there's dedicated debug hardware that can actually stop the core, read and write memory and registers, and compare the program counter against breakpoint addresses.
A hardware breakpoint works because a comparator watches the instruction fetch address. When it matches, the core halts and the debugger reads everything out.
Chips only have a few of these comparators, typically four to eight. Besides finding bugs, the same connection is used to program the flash.
The limitation is that halting is intrusive, so for something like a motor controller or a radio you can't just pause the system.
In those cases I use trace, GPIO toggles or logging along with the debugger."
